summary: Whiteface's summit steel tower, dismantled in 1972 and re-erected in 1973, now stands as an outdoor exhibit at the Adirondack Museum on Blue Mountain Lake.

facts.design: Steel lookout tower with a glass-enclosed cab; sources give 22 feet (1919) and about 50 feet (1942)

access.note: Outdoor exhibit on the grounds of the Adirondack Museum (Adirondack Experience) at Blue Mountain Lake. The sources read do not say whether the cab can be climbed or what admission applies.

events.note: A state observation station was established on the summit in July 1909 with a pole frame and canvas tent and no tower at first. The 1910 state report gives the cost as $1,559.31.
Sam Cheltham was fire observer until November 1, 1918, and was back on the job by May 1919.
A 22-foot steel Aermotor LS40 tower replaced the log-pole station. A 1972 newspaper item instead calls the dismantled tower built in 1909.
George Marshall was the state fire observer on Whiteface.
A new observer's cabin was built on the summit, to the standard 12 by 16 foot cabin plan the state had just adopted.
Five caddy boys damaged a window sash in the observation room. A district ranger let them off if they bought a new sash, which they did.
A CCC crew drilled holes in the rocky peak for steel poles, part of a new telephone line from the base to the tower.
The marker page says a stone observation tower built in 1935 supplanted the steel tower. The 1942 description and the 1972 item conflict with this.
A Coast and Geodetic Survey description calls the tower a structural steel lookout about 50 feet high.
Riley Lawrence was fire observer on the state tower for the rest of the season. U.S. weather observers also worked on the peak.
The steel tower was dismantled in May 1972 under a wilderness plan. A newspaper item from that month says the tower had been taken apart and lay in about 200 pieces.
Re-erected at the Adirondack Museum on Blue Mountain Lake.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The marker inscription and a 1972 newspaper item say 1909. The marker text and the 1919 items date the steel tower to 1919, and the marker text says the 1909 station had no tower until then. The record and story treat 1909 as the station's start and 1919 as the steel tower's build year.

notes_for_editor: Height conflict: 22 feet (1919 items and marker text) against about 50 feet (1942 Coast and Geodetic Survey description). Not resolved; facts.height_m is omitted and the design fact gives both. Build year conflict: 1909 (marker inscription, 1972 item) against 1919 (marker text, 1919 items); see resolved_conflicts. The marker says a 1935 stone tower supplanted the steel tower, but the 1942 description and the 1972 item describe steel on the summit later, so the 1935 claim is recorded as a conflict. Removal date: May 1972 newspaper item and marker text agree on 1972. A search snippet suggested 1971 from another site; that page was not read, so it is not used. Visitor climbing rules and admission are not in the sources read; a search snippet mentioned museum admission, but that page was not read, so it is not used. The record had no height or built year; the events add 1919 and 1909 with conflict notes. No photos added (no image URLs read).
